newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Donors pledge $1.94 billion aid to Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: Donors pledge $1.94 billion aid to Bangladesh.

text.p: The new Bangladesh government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Friday claimed credit for winning an increased pledge of $1.94 billion from donors despite the adverse aid climate.

"Although the rate of assistance is falling in an unfavourable international aid climate, Bangladesh could muster donors' support for a higher commitment this year," Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria told reporters on his return from a donors' meeting in Paris.
Kibria said the initiatives by the new government to encourage the private sector had a positive impact on the donors at the Paris meeting this week.
"This is the first time the donors have not attached any string to aid. We would not have accepted such things," he said.

But World Bank Vice-President Joseph Wood, who chaired the Paris meeting, said: "Unless there is substantial progress in implementing the government's reforms agenda and steady improvement in aid utilisation, the development partners (donors) indicated that future aid flows are likely to fall."
Wood, however, said: "This level of support is remarkable, given the deterioratioon in the general aid climate and Bangladesh's poor aid utilisation record."

"The government's objective is to raise the GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth rate to 7.0 to 8.0 percent, a target which the donors endorsed as necessary to reduce significantly poverty within a reasonable timeframe," he said.

Bangladesh's GDP grew at 4.7 percent in 1995/96 against 4.4 percent the previous year. Nearly half of the country's 119.7 million people live below the poverty line. Per capita annual income is about $260.

Finance Ministry officials said on Friday that Bangladesh had received only $1.45 billion in foreign aid in 1995/96 against a commitment of $1.9 billion. The country expected aid disbursement at $1.7 billion in the current year, they said.
"Donors did ask for speedy reforms, but it's the first time they have not set a timeframe for that," Kibria said.
The reforms would be implemented in phases. "We will not do it hastily to create upheavals in the society," he said.
